summary: Appwrite's API, a PHP 8.5 and Swoole monolith, is moving to Rust one service at a time. First every Utopia library it stands on is converted and proven identical to PHP, then each API service is ported and run side by side with PHP behind Traefik, on the same database, Redis, queues and caches.

facts.label: compat cases
facts.note: Recorded from PHP and replayed against Rust, across 54 libraries (778,267 steps).

facts.label: database cases
facts.note: utopia-database 8.3.0 alone, recorded from PHP over Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, SQLite, MongoDB and Redis; 557 of 557 PHP test files ported.

facts.label: Users scenarios identical
facts.note: The PHP vs Rust parity diff: responses, database deltas and Redis effects compared per identity, origin and request variant.

facts.label: differences on the Users API
facts.note: After the database 8 upgrade, down from 290 when PHP moved first.

facts.label: throughput
facts.note: 2,758 vs 1,045 requests per second with 50 virtual users on an Apple M4 Max, 0 failures on either side.

facts.label: less CPU per request
facts.note: 0.76 vs 4.34 ms of API CPU per request at 200 requests per second.

facts.label: less memory
facts.note: 58 MiB vs 1,957 MiB average at 200 requests per second.

facts.label: lower median latency
facts.note: 1.5 vs 6.3 ms p50 at 200 requests per second; p99 12.5 vs 23.5 ms.

facts.label: a rewrite, followed
facts.note: main moved utopia-php/database from 7.4 to 8.1.3, close to a rewrite, then to 8.3.0 two days later; the Rust port, its adapters and every crate that uses it followed both times.

facts.label: database and query tests
facts.note: Rust unit and integration tests in utopia-database and utopia-query.

facts.label: engines
facts.note: Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, SQLite, MongoDB on the official Rust driver, and Redis, plus Memory, Pool and Mirror (replicating every write to a second database).

facts.label: cache keys
facts.note: PHP and Rust share one Redis cache and one igbinary format, so every cache key and entry must match PHP to the byte.

facts.label: commits on the branch
facts.note: Since it last left main, between 2026-10-09 and 2026-10-15.

facts.label: one area each
facts.note: Claude Code agents in separate git worktrees: core, SQL adapters, Mongo, PHP harness, Rust harness, each service; merged and verified by one coordinating session.

facts.label: CI last
facts.note: Every change verified locally (tests, clippy on CI's Rust 1.88, the compat lanes) before a single push; CI checked at milestones.

timeline.note: Each converted library gets a benchmark beside its PHP original, published on this site.

timeline.note: A fresh-stack benchmark on a quiet machine; then abuse limits, sessions, MFA, custom-domain CORS and the database listeners in appwrite-core.

timeline.note: 13 Teams routes and about 88 Account routes ported; the parity matrix at 2,135 of 2,135.

timeline.note: PHP's database rewrite followed in Rust: core, six engines, migration, audit, usage, the Appwrite crates and both sides of the compat harness.

timeline.note: main moved on while the port caught up: http, usage, queue and migration synced with their packages on main (migration: 284 cases, 0 differences), and utopia-php/database moved again, to 8.3.0.

timeline.title: utopia-database 8.3.0 and Mirror
timeline.note: Race-free bulk deletes, relationship queries with per-parent paging, typed aggregates, and Mirror, the last part of the library, ported; every database case re-recorded on 8.3.0.

lessons: Prove, don't port: a library counts as converted only when every PHP test class is ported and recorded PHP results replay identically in Rust, fuzzed inputs included.
PHP's quirks are the spec. php-std reproduces Zend's sort, PCRE2's JIT limits, ext-yaml and igbinary, because Appwrite's data depends on them.
Share state, not code: both runtimes use one database, one Redis and one cache, so routes can move between them one at a time and back.
Sync often: in one day main moved four of the PHP packages the port follows; drift shows up first as compat differences in CI, which is the earliest place to catch it.
A moving target: the PHP side keeps changing on main, so the compat recordings are regenerated from PHP whenever a dependency moves, and Rust follows.
Watch the tooling, too: wait loops that poll for a log line outlive the work they wait on; background commands that report when they exit do not.
Run the comparison on the stack CI runs: a parity diff that was clean on a hand-patched local stack showed 44 differences on CI's, from one environment variable given to only one runtime.
